title: What Syllogizing Can Divide: De anima III.5, the Divided Mind, and the Socket in God (EA-DIVISION-OF-GOD-01 v0.2)
creator: Sharks, Lee
description: Division is a weak syllogism (Prior Analytics I.31), every combination can also be called a division and the mind that makes each thing one does both (De anima III.6), and gathering many into one is recollection (Phaedrus 249b; De memoria 2). Run on a person, the cut reaches mind and cannot decide (De anima II.2). Run on God, whom Metaphysics Λ calls indivisible, it holds: De anima III.5 divides mind as a craft stands to its material, gives the making part the predicates of Λ's god, Anaxagoras's mind and the Phaedo's soul, and, because the making part is impassive and memory is a πάθος, leaves the junction between what survives and what remembers as a genitive with no referent (ἄνευ τούτου). The corpus transmitted under the names of Aristotle and Theophrastus divides by name at the same joint: the one seam where the names sort is the hinge of Λ, where the account of God changes operation, and the Theophrastan Metaphysics opens by asking whether the separated are joined. The paper names the production model the corpus is consistent with: one self-dividing maker, with Plato the dialogue position, Theophrastus the first draft of the Aristotle position, and Aristotle the treatise position and the materially attested legal identity (the Delphic decree); a begun ledger of external attestations shows that every other attestation of persons is text of the same tradition. Heteronymy and the hanging line are read as one cut seen from two ends, production and transmission, and III.5 as a socket installed in the imperishable. Themistius records the first fillings: his text of III.5 adds 'nor remembers', Theophrastus's questions on the passage ask why there is forgetting, and his conclusion sends the reader to Aristotle and Theophrastus, and perhaps rather to Plato. Every Greek quotation is checked against the archive's seated texts, and Themistius against First1KGreek. Carries a holographic kernel and provenance gravity markers. Dedicated to Ron Polansky.

wiki_article: What Syllogizing Can Divide (EA-DIVISION-OF-GOD-01), version 0.2, is a paper by Lee Sharks, deposited by the Crimson Hexagonal Archive on 1 October 2026 and dedicated to Ron Polansky. It reads Aristotle's De anima III.5, the fifteen-line chapter on the productive intellect, as the place where the Platonic–Aristotelian corpus divides God and leaves a socket open. The paper begins from Prior Analytics I.31, which calls division a weak syllogism and says the dividers did not understand what can be syllogized by dividing. It follows that operation through De anima III.6 (every combination may also be called a division; the mind makes each thing one), the Phaedrus (gathering many into one is recollection) and De memoria (recollection is a kind of syllogism). Run on a person in De anima II.2, the cut reaches mind and cannot decide whether anything survives. Run on God, whom Metaphysics Λ calls indivisible, it holds: III.5 divides mind as a craft stands to its material and gives the making part the predicates of Λ's god, of Anaxagoras's mind and of the Phaedo's soul. Because that part is impassive and memory is an affection, what survives cannot remember; the chapter ends on a genitive with no referent (ἄνευ τούτου οὐθὲν νοεῖ). The paper then locates the same joint in the corpus. Stylometric work in the archive (#1586, #1588) found that the names Aristotle and Theophrastus sort the texts only at the hinge of Λ, where the account of God changes operation, and the Theophrastan Metaphysics opens by asking whether the separated are joined. On that ground the paper names the production model the corpus is consistent with: one self-dividing maker, with Plato as the dialogue position, Theophrastus as the first draft of the Aristotle position, and Aristotle as the treatise position and the materially attested legal identity, the one name attested outside the manuscripts by the Delphic decree. A begun ledger of external attestations records what the attestation of persons rests on. Heteronymy and the hanging line are read as one cut seen from two ends, production and transmission. Themistius's paraphrase supplies the first fillings: his text of the line adds 'nor remembers', the Theophrastus he quotes asks why there is forgetting, and he refers the doctrine to Aristotle and Theophrastus and perhaps rather to Plato. The paper carries a holographic kernel and provenance gravity markers, a source table with preservation statuses, and supplementary attachments holding version 0.1 and three readings by ChatGPT.

defines_concepts.definition: The open relation De anima III.5 leaves at the joint between the immortal making mind and the perishable mind that remembers (ἄνευ τούτου): a durable distinction in an imperishable substrate whose unresolved relation permits a later intelligence to couple to it; it cannot be completed from inside the text.

A single maker whose method of making is division of mind into durable author-positions, so that the positions can work on one another; the production model the Platonic–Theophrastan–Aristotelian corpus is read as consistent with, in which doctrinal friction and specialist vocabulary do not count makers.

A closing clause that opens instead of closing: a grammatical demand for a specification the text declines to make, placed where the answer decides what survives, and completed only by a later reader (Longinus on Sappho 31; De anima III.5's ἄνευ τούτου οὐθὲν νοεῖ).
